intro: In this college you'll learn how to do your groceries in Dutch: name the shops, ask where things are, offer and ask for help, request quantities politely, ask the price, and check whether a shop is open.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — shopping every day
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme two. Its title is [[Boodschappen doen]], which means 'doing the groceries'. This is one of the most useful themes in your whole course, because you go shopping almost every day, and every trip is a tiny Dutch conversation. The word for groceries is [[de boodschappen]], and the activity of getting them is [[boodschappen doen]]. A Dutch person might say [[Ik ga even boodschappen doen]], 'I'm just popping out to do the groceries'. The general word for a shop is [[de winkel]], and the big self-service food shop is [[de supermarkt]]. The two most famous supermarkets in the Netherlands are Albert Heijn, which everyone simply calls [[de Appie]], and Jumbo. There is also the open-air [[de markt]], the market, usually once a week on a square in your town, where fruit, vegetables and cheese are often cheaper and fresher. As always in this college, I explain in English, but every Dutch word and sentence is spoken by a native voice, so please repeat each phrase out loud after me. That is how your mouth learns the sounds. Ready to go shopping? [[Laten we beginnen!]]

paragraphs.heading: The shops and what you buy there
paragraphs.text: Let's learn where you buy things. For bread you go to the baker, [[de bakker]], and you buy [[het brood]], bread, and small rolls called [[de broodjes]]. Notice that little ending: one roll is [[een broodje]], two or more are [[twee broodjes]] — Dutch often makes plurals by adding 's' or 'en'. For meat you visit the butcher, [[de slager]]; for medicine the chemist, [[de drogist]] or the pharmacy, [[de apotheek]]. Inside the supermarket you grab a basket, [[een mandje]], or a trolley, [[een winkelwagen]]. The main food groups are easy and high-frequency: vegetables are [[de groente]], fruit is [[het fruit]], and milk is [[de melk]]. Common items in your basket might be [[de appels]], apples; [[de aardappelen]], potatoes; [[de eieren]], eggs; and [[de kaas]], cheese. Household things matter too, like [[het wasmiddel]], laundry detergent, and [[het toiletpapier]], toilet paper. When you pay, you go to the checkout, [[de kassa]]. A handy tip: in the Netherlands you often pay a small deposit on bottles, called [[het statiegeld]], and you get it back by returning the empty bottles to a machine in the shop. So keep those bottles!

paragraphs.heading: Offering and asking for help
paragraphs.text: Shops are full of friendly little exchanges, so let's learn them. When you walk in, an assistant, [[de verkoper]] or [[de verkoopster]], may offer help with [[Kan ik u helpen?]], 'Can I help you?'. If you are just browsing, you answer politely [[Nee, dank u, ik kijk even rond]], 'No thank you, I'm just looking around'. When you do need help, the magic question is [[Kunt u mij helpen?]], 'Can you help me?'. To find a product, ask [[Waar vind ik de melk?]], 'Where do I find the milk?', or more simply [[Waar is het brood?]], 'Where is the bread?'. To check if they stock something, use [[Heeft u ook verse vis?]], 'Do you also have fresh fish?'. Notice that polite word [[u]] again — in a shop with a stranger, you almost always use [[u]], not [[je]]. Two more golden sentences for beginners: if the assistant speaks too fast, say [[Kunt u langzamer praten?]], 'Can you speak more slowly?', and if you miss something, [[Kunt u dat herhalen?]], 'Can you repeat that?'. Dutch shopkeepers are used to learners, so do not be shy. When you are finished, a warm way to close is [[Dat is alles, dank u]], 'That's everything, thank you'.

paragraphs.heading: Polite requests and quantities
paragraphs.text: Now the heart of shopping: asking for what you want, politely. The most useful pattern starts with the words 'ik wil graag', meaning 'I would like'. That little word [[graag]] turns a blunt 'I want' into a warm 'I would like', so always include it. For example [[Ik wil graag een kilo appels]], 'I would like a kilo of apples'. An even more polite opener begins with 'mag ik', literally 'may I', as in [[Mag ik een halve kilo kaas?]], 'May I have half a kilo of cheese?'. For quantities you often need no article at all: [[een kilo aardappelen]], a kilo of potatoes; [[een pak melk]], a carton of milk; and [[zes eieren]], six eggs. Notice the plurals after a number — [[appels]], [[aardappelen]], [[eieren]] — while mass words like [[melk]] and [[kaas]] stay singular. At a cheese or meat counter you will hear a charming question: [[Mag het een onsje meer zijn?]], which asks if it can be a little more, an [[onsje]] being about a hundred grams. You just answer [[Ja, dat is prima]], 'Yes, that's fine'. And to take a set number of something, point and say [[Doet u er maar twee]], 'I'll take two, please'.

paragraphs.heading: Prices, opening hours, and paying
paragraphs.text: Let's talk money and time. To ask a price, the key question is [[Hoeveel kost het?]], 'How much does it cost?', or pointing at an item, [[Hoeveel kost dit?]]. For a quantity you might ask [[Hoeveel kost een kilo tomaten?]], 'How much does a kilo of tomatoes cost?'. Look out for a special offer, [[de aanbieding]], and if something is cheap a Dutch person happily says [[Dat is een koopje!]], 'That's a bargain!'. When it is time to pay you go to [[de kassa]], the till, and almost everyone pays by debit card. The verb is [[pinnen]], so you ask [[Kan ik met pin betalen?]], 'Can I pay by debit card?'. Many small shops and market stalls are card-only now, so do not rely on cash. Opening hours are [[de openingstijden]], and this matters in the Netherlands because shops often close earlier than you expect. Ask [[Hoe laat gaat de winkel dicht?]], 'What time does the shop close?', and [[Hoe laat gaat de winkel open?]], 'What time does it open?'. To check a specific day, use [[er is]] and [[er zijn]] style questions like [[Is de supermarkt op zondag open?]], 'Is the supermarket open on Sunday?'. If you see [[De winkel is gesloten]], that simply means 'The shop is closed'.

paragraphs.heading: A mini-scene — and well done
paragraphs.text: Let's put it all together at the cheese counter. The assistant smiles and says [[Goedemiddag, kan ik u helpen?]], 'Good afternoon, can I help you?'. You answer [[Ja, graag. Ik wil graag wat jonge kaas]], 'Yes please, I'd like some young cheese'. He asks [[Hoeveel wilt u hebben?]], 'How much would you like?', and you say [[Een halve kilo, alstublieft]], 'Half a kilo, please'. He weighs it and asks [[Mag het iets meer zijn?]], 'Can it be a little more?', and you reply [[Ja, dat is prima]]. Then you check the shelf with [[er zijn]] thinking: [[Zijn er ook olijven?]], 'Are there olives too?'. He points and says [[Ja, daar in de koeling]], 'Yes, over there in the cooler'. You finish with [[Nee, dat was het. Kan ik met pin betalen?]], 'No, that was it. Can I pay by card?'. He nods: [[Ja hoor, bij de kassa. Een fijne dag nog!]], 'Yes of course, at the till. Have a nice day!'. That is a complete, real shopping conversation, and you now have every piece of it. Practise it out loud today during your own boodschappen. [[Heel goed gedaan!]] Well done — I'll see you in theme three!
